perf.summary: Hoist b-column access into row-major form and reduce modulo frequency to cut the modulo-per-multiply cost and improve cache behavior in the innermost k-loop.
perf.currentCost: Inner loop does b[k*n+j] (column-strided, cache-unfriendly: stride n*8 bytes) plus one 64-bit modulo per k iteration. For n^3 inner iterations that is n^3 divisions and n^3 strided loads -> heavy DIV-port pressure and TLB/cache misses.
perf.proposedChange: Reorder loops to i-k-j (cache-friendly: stream b row b[k*n+j] sequentially, accumulate into tmp row tmp[i*n+j]). Compute aik=a[i*n+k] once per (i,k), and apply % mod once after the j-accumulation pass per element rather than every k step where the running sum cannot overflow. Concretely: since mod fits in long and inputs are already reduced (< mod), if mod <= ~3037000499 (sqrt(2^63)) then a[i*n+k]*b[k*n+j] < 2^63 and sum stays bounded by reducing only when sum could overflow; otherwise keep per-step %. Minimum safe win: keep per-step % but switch to i-k-j ordering with aik hoisted, eliminating the column-strided b access and the repeated a[i*n+k] index recomputation.
perf.rationale: i-k-j ordering turns the inner loop into two sequential streams (b row, tmp row) that Burst/SLP can vectorize and the prefetcher loves, versus the current i-j-k which reads a column of b with stride n. Hoisting aik removes one multiply-add address computation per inner iteration. Both lower cycles and cache misses with identical numeric results when % is kept per step.
perf.risk: i-k-j reordering with per-step % is bit-exact identical to i-j-k per-step % because (sum + x) % mod is applied after each add regardless of accumulation order ONLY IF the same set of products is summed in the same order; i-k-j changes summation order. Modular addition is associative/commutative so the final residue is identical, but intermediate values differ — final result provably equal mod p. Deferring the % (the overflow-conditional variant) is only safe when mod*mod + mod < 2^63 (mod < ~3.03e9) AND inputs pre-reduced; must guard with a named constant MaxDeferMod or reject. Signed long products of pre-reduced non-negative residues stay non-negative, no signed-% pitfall.

perf.summary: Eliminate the per-call stackalloc scratch buffer and the trailing MemoryCopy by writing the product into a caller-provided ping-pong buffer.
perf.currentCost: Each MultiplyMatrices does stackalloc long[n*n] (grows stack per call inside a loop-driven recursion-free path; repeated stackalloc in the squaring loop reuses frame but still zero-inits cost is avoided, yet the n*n*8-byte MemoryCopy at the end is a full extra pass over the matrix every multiply).
perf.proposedChange: Hoist two n*n buffers in Run (src/dst) and ping-pong: MultiplyMatrices writes result into dst and the caller swaps pointers, removing the final Buffer.MemoryCopy(tmp,a,...) entirely. Pass dst as an out pointer; Run already owns temp and result, just add a second temp for squaring.
perf.rationale: Removes one full n*n*8-byte memory pass (the copy-back) per matrix multiply. In matrix-pow there are O(log exp) squarings plus up to log exp products, so eliminating the copy saves O(n^2 log exp) writes. Also avoids re-stackallocing scratch on every call.
perf.risk: Pointer ping-pong must keep result semantics: final answer must end up in the caller's result buffer. Need a final conditional copy only if the last write landed in the scratch buffer (one copy total vs one-per-multiply). Behavior identical; care needed that MultiplyMatrices(temp,temp,...) self-multiply still reads consistent source (already needs scratch because output overlaps input — ping-pong naturally fixes the aliasing).

perf.summary: Replace the branchy double loop with a zero-fill plus diagonal write to remove n^2 branches.
perf.currentCost: n^2 iterations each evaluating (i==j)?1:0 — a data-dependent branch/cmov per element across the whole matrix.
perf.proposedChange: memset/loop-zero the n*n block (or Unsafe.InitBlock / a tight for writing 0), then a single diagonal loop: for(int i=0;i<n;i++) res[i*n+i]=1. Diagonal index i*n+i can be strength-reduced with an accumulator idx+=n+1.
perf.rationale: Turns n^2 conditional writes into a branchless contiguous zero-fill (vectorizable / single InitBlock) plus n diagonal writes. Fewer instructions, no per-element compare, prefetcher-friendly contiguous store.
perf.risk: None — output identical. InitBlock requires byte count n*n*sizeof(long); ensure no overflow of the int byte-count argument for large n (n*n*8 must fit int; guard or use loop for very large n).

perf.summary: Hoist the repeated trans[f*alphabetSize+i] and fail[next] computations and force inlining of this hot per-edge helper.
perf.currentCost: trans[f*alphabetSize+i] is computed twice (loop condition and after the loop at line 75), and fail[next] is read twice (lines 75-76: fail[next] is written then re-read). state*alphabetSize+i recomputed at lines 70 and 81. The method is a non-inlined call invoked alphabetSize times per dequeued state in the BFS hot loop.
perf.proposedChange: Add [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)] to ProcessTransition (and InitializeRootTransitions). Cache long baseIdx=state*alphabetSize+i once. After the while loop, store the resolved target t=trans[f*alphabetSize+i] in a local, write fail[next]=t and use t (not a re-read of fail[next]) for output[next]|=output[t].
perf.rationale: Removes a redundant load+multiply-add per edge, shortens the dependency chain (output|= no longer waits on a reload of fail[next]), and inlining eliminates call overhead and lets Burst keep base indices in registers across the whole alphabet loop. Asymptotics unchanged but constant factor on the dominant BFS edge loop drops.
perf.risk: Behavior-preserving: fail[next] is set to exactly trans[f*alphabetSize+i] so reusing the local t for output is identical. Inlining a recursive-free leaf is safe under Burst. No aliasing issue since next!=state in Aho-Corasick goto edges (next is a distinct child state).

perf.summary: The else-branch mutates trans in place to build the goto-automaton, mixing two responsibilities; splitting the failure-link build from the goto-completion would clarify the API but is optional.
perf.currentCost: Single helper both (a) computes failure links for real edges and (b) path-compresses missing edges via trans[state*A+i]=trans[fail[state]*A+i]. The dual role makes the hot method harder to reason about and prevents the compiler from specializing each path.
perf.proposedChange: Keep the perf model but consider documenting that this is the standard Aho-Corasick BFS goto-completion; optionally precompute fail[state] into a local fs once at method entry (used in both branches) to avoid two fail[state] loads.
perf.rationale: fail[state] is loaded in both branches (line 73 and 81); hoisting it to a single local at entry removes one load on the else path and clarifies intent. Minor cycle + readability win.
perf.risk: None — fail[state] is not modified within the method, so a single cached load is identical to two loads.
